transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ___; what brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. ___. I'm here because... well, things at work have been really hard lately. I'm a hairstylist, you know? And lately, my hands just feel like they’re moving through glue. Like, even just sectioning hair or mixing color, it takes me forever now. It's so frustrating because I used to be really fast. I remember this one time, I had three clients booked at the same time—a cut, a color, and a blowout—and I just breezed through it. My manager even bought me a coffee afterward because she was so impressed. I love iced coffee, by the way, especially with oat milk. Regular milk just upsets my stomach. Anyway, yeah, people have started noticing I’m just slower than I used to be. My coworker, Jessica, she asked me if I was tired the other day, and she's usually so focused on her own station, she never notices anything. She has this huge collection of vintage shears, it's wild. But yeah, I'm just so slow now.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you been feeling down, depressed, or hopeless most days?

Yeah, I have. Most days I just wake up with this... this heavy, flat sadness right in my chest. It just weighs me down before I even get out of bed. It really feels like there’s no point in trying to build the life I was planning, you know? I always wanted to open my own little bridal styling studio by the time I was 25. I even had a whole Pinterest board for the decor. I was going to paint the walls this really soft sage green because green is supposed to be super calming. My aunt had a green kitchen when I was growing up, and she used to bake these incredible lemon bars in there. Honestly, I haven't had a good lemon bar in years. The ones at the bakery next to my salon are always way too sweet, and they put so much powdered sugar on top that it gets all over your black work clothes... and you can't be covered in powdered sugar when you're trying to do a color consultation with a client. Wait, what was I saying? But yeah, just... really sad and hopeless most days.
Has this low mood been going on for at least two years?

Two years? No, I don't think it's been quite that long. It’s been more like... about a year and two months now with this heavy depression. I know because it started right around the time I bought my new shears. They're these beautiful rose-gold ones, Japanese steel. They cut like absolute butter. You really have to invest in good tools if you're doing hair every day, otherwise your wrists get completely wrecked. Carpal tunnel is like the number one thing stylists complain about, well, besides clients who lie about using box dye. Oh my gosh, people will sit right in your chair and swear they haven't colored their hair in five years, and then you put lightener on it and it turns bright orange. It's like, just tell me! I can fix it, but I need to know what's under there. Box dye has these metallic salts in it, which can literally melt your hair if you're not careful. I've seen it actually smoke in the foil before, it's terrifying. You have to rinse it immediately. But um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the timeline. Yeah, just a year and two months of feeling this way.
Have you started, stopped, or changed any medications or substances around the time this depression began?

No, I haven't changed any medications or anything like that. I don't really take much, just vitamins sometimes. I tried taking these gummy vitamins for hair, skin, and nails a while ago because a lot of my clients were asking if they actually work. They taste just like candy, which is dangerous because you're only supposed to eat two, but you want to eat a whole handful. They're strawberry flavored, I think. Strawberries are actually my favorite fruit, especially in the summer when you can get them fresh from the farmer's market. There's this one guy at the market downtown who sells the biggest strawberries I've ever seen, they're like the size of apples. My roommate and I used to go every Sunday morning, but she moved out a few months ago to live with her boyfriend. He's a mechanic, and he's always coming home with grease under his fingernails. It drives me crazy because I'm so used to everything having to be perfectly clean and sanitized at the salon. We have to soak all our combs in Barbicide after every single client. It's this bright blue liquid, and it smells really strong, kind of like a swimming pool but more chemical. But anyway, no, no new medications or substances or anything when the sadness started.
Do you worry excessively about a lot of different things most days?

Worry? I mean, I guess I worry a normal amount, but I wouldn't say it's excessive or about a ton of different things every single day. I do worry about my clients' hair sometimes, though. Like, if they want to go from dark brown to platinum blonde in one session. That is so stressful because you really have to lift it slowly or the hair just snaps off. Breakage is the absolute worst. We had this one client last month who tried to bleach her own hair at home with 40 volume developer, which you should never, ever do on your scalp. Her hair literally felt like cotton candy, just mushy and stretchy. We had to do a massive protein treatment, like Olaplex step one and two, and then cut off at least four inches. She was crying, and I felt so bad, but honestly, it looked so much healthier as a bob. Bobs are actually really coming back into style right now, especially the blunt, French-girl bobs with the little fringe. I was thinking about cutting my own hair like that, but my face is a little too round for it. My mom always told me I had a moon face when I was little. She meant it in a cute way, I think, but kids can be so mean about that kind of stuff. I remember this one boy in third grade... wait, what was the question? Oh, worrying. No, I don't think I worry about a bunch of different things all the time. Just normal stuff, mostly.
Have you had these symptoms for most of the day, on more days than not, continuously during the past two years?

Continuous for two years? Um, no, like I said earlier, it's really only been about a year and two months that I've been feeling this low. It definitely hasn't been two whole years. Two years ago I was still in cosmetology school, actually. That was such a crazy time. We had to practice on these mannequin heads for months before they let us touch real people. They're so creepy, especially when you walk into the classroom early in the morning and there are just fifty decapitated heads staring at you from the counters. Some of the girls used to draw makeup on them with Sharpie, which the instructors hated because it stains the plastic forever. One time, my friend Jessica accidentally melted her mannequin's hair with a curling iron because it was synthetic and she had the heat turned all the way up to 400 degrees. The smell was horrendous, like burning tires and plastic. We had to open all the windows, and it was the middle of January, so we were all freezing in our smocks. Smocks are so unflattering, by the way. They make everyone look like a black rectangle. But yeah, no, not two years. Just the year and a bit.
During the past two years, has there ever been a stretch of at least two months when you felt back to your usual self?

Two months? Um... I don't think so. I haven't really felt like myself for a long time now. Even when I have an okay day, it never lasts for two whole months. Two months is a long time. That's like, almost a whole season. I love when the seasons change, especially fall. Fall is the absolute best time for hair color. Everyone wants to go warmer, you know? Like rich chocolate browns, copper, auburn... it's so gorgeous. The formulas are so fun to mix, it's like painting. We did this one girl last week, she wanted this 'cowboy copper' trend that's all over TikTok right now. Have you seen it? It's like this dusty, muted red-brown. It looked amazing on her, she had these green eyes that just popped. Green eyes are so pretty. My cat has green eyes. His name is Barnaby, and he's a rescue. He's super fluffy, but he sheds everywhere. I have to lint roll my clothes like three times before I leave the house, because you can't show up to the salon covered in cat hair. It just looks unprofessional. Clients notice that stuff. They notice everything, honestly. Like if your nails aren't done, or if your roots are grown out. It's a lot of pressure to always look perfect. But um... yeah, no, I haven't had a good stretch like that in a long time.
Have you ever had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energized or needed much less sleep than usual?

Energized? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm pretty tired most of the time lately. I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get at least eight hours, I am basically a zombie at the salon. And you cannot be a zombie when you're holding sharp shears right next to someone's ear, you know? It's actually really scary how sharp professional shears are. They're made of this Japanese steel, usually, and they cost like, hundreds of dollars. My first pair was $300, and that was with my student discount. You have to get them sharpened by this special guy who comes to the salon once a month with a little mobile workshop in his van. He's this older guy named Gary, and he always brings donuts. Glazed donuts, which are my favorite, but I try not to eat them because I'm trying to cut back on sugar. Sugar just makes my skin break out so bad, especially around my chin. I read somewhere that chin breakouts are hormonal, but I don't know. Skin care is so confusing. There are a million different serums and acids now. Hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic... it's overwhelming. Sometimes I just want to wash my face with regular soap, but my esthetician friend would actually murder me if I did that. She says bar soap destroys your skin barrier. But yeah, no, I've never had a time where I didn't need sleep or felt super energized like that. Just tired.
Have you had any medical illness or injury involving your brain, like a head injury, stroke, seizure disorder, or thyroid problem?

Um, no, nothing like that. I've never had a stroke or a seizure or anything wrong with my brain like that. I did hit my head on a cabinet door at the salon once, though. Someone left it open—probably Sarah, she's always leaving the color bar cabinets wide open—and I just stood up right into it. It hurt so bad, I actually saw stars for a second. But I didn't go to the doctor or anything, I just put some ice on it. The ice machine at work is always broken, by the way. It makes this horrible grinding noise, like it's chewing on rocks, and then it just spits out water instead of cubes. We've told the owner, Mr. Davis, like five times, but he's so cheap. He hates spending money on maintenance. He wouldn't even fix the AC last summer until three clients complained that they were sweating through their capes. Those capes get so hot anyway, they don't breathe at all. It's like wearing a trash bag. We try to use the lightweight ones, but they still trap all your body heat. Anyway, no, I haven't had any major head injuries or thyroid things. My thyroid is fine, as far as I know.
Before this current period of depression, have you ever had another episode of feeling this depressed for at least two weeks?

Um, no, I don't think so. Not before this current time. I mean, I've had bad days here and there, but never two whole weeks in a row of feeling this down. Two weeks is actually exactly how long I tell my clients to wait if they try to cut their own hair at home and mess it up. You know, give it two weeks to grow out just a tiny bit so I have something to work with to fix it. Especially bangs. People get a little sad or bored at 2 AM and suddenly decide they need micro-bangs, and it's always a disaster. Everyone thinks they want bangs right now, like those really cute curtain bangs, but they don't realize how much styling it takes. You have to use a round brush and a blow dryer every single morning, or they just lay flat against your forehead and look super greasy. I always try to warn them, but they never listen. They just bring in a picture from Pinterest and say, 'I want this,' and I have to explain that the girl in the picture has a professional stylist and perfect lighting. Lighting changes everything. We have this huge ring light at the salon for taking Instagram photos of our work, and if you stand in front of it without makeup, you look completely washed out. I actually had to buy this special color-correcting primer just so I wouldn't look dead in the background of my coworkers' photos. It's green, which is so weird to put on your face, but it cancels out the redness. Color theory is actually super interesting, it's basically the whole foundation of doing hair color. But um... what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I haven't had a two-week stretch of feeling like this before.
Before this current depression, have you ever had another episode like this that lasted at least two weeks?

Um, I... I think you just asked me that, didn't you? Or wait, did you? My brain is just so foggy right now. But no, I haven't. Not before this time. It's just been this one really long stretch. Kind of like when a client wants to go from box-dye black to platinum blonde in one session. It's just this long, agonizing process, and you're just sitting there waiting for the bleach to lift, hoping their hair doesn't melt off in the foils. Because box dye is the absolute worst. It has all these metallic salts in it that react with professional lightener, and it literally smokes. I saw a girl's hair start smoking once in beauty school. The instructor had to rush over and rinse it out in the bowl, and the smell was horrendous. It smelled like burning tires and sulfur. The bowl area in beauty school was always a mess anyway. The drains were constantly clogged with hair because nobody ever cleaned the traps. It's so gross pulling out those wet clumps of hair. But yeah, no, I haven't had another time like this before. Just this one.
Have there ever been times during this past year and two months when you felt depressed for at least two months at a stretch?

Um, yeah, I'd say so. Looking back on it, I've spent most of this whole time... like this whole decline over the last year or whatever... feeling really depressed and just weighed down. There were only short stretches where the sadness wasn't as prominent. It's just so heavy, you know? Like when you try to lift a gallon of developer. We buy developer in these massive jugs at the salon to save money, mostly 20 volume because that's what we use the most of for gray coverage. Gray hair is so stubborn. It lacks pigment, obviously, but the cuticle is also super tight, so you really have to pack the color on and sometimes use heat to open it up. A lot of women come in every four weeks on the dot to get their roots touched up. They hate seeing that skunk stripe down their part. I had this one client, Mrs. Higgins, she would come in every three weeks. She was terrified of anyone knowing she wasn't a natural redhead. Red fades the fastest, too. The color molecules are larger than other colors, so they literally slip right out of the hair shaft every time you wash it. That's why I always tell my redheads to wash in cold water. But who wants to take a freezing cold shower? Especially in the winter. Our water heater at my apartment is terrible, so I end up taking cold showers half the time anyway. It takes like twenty minutes for the water to even get lukewarm. But um... yeah, mostly I've just been really depressed this whole time, with only small breaks.
Do you often feel like a failure or feel bad about yourself?

Yeah, all the time. I just... I keep thinking I'm a burden on everyone. Like I completely deserve all of this happening to me because I couldn't even keep my money straight or hold onto my job. I couldn't even manage basic salon responsibilities, you know? Like sweeping up hair or keeping my station sanitized. State board is so strict about sanitation. If an inspector walks in and sees a single hair on your clippers or a comb sitting on the counter instead of in the Barbicide, they can fine you on the spot. The Barbicide jar has to be changed every single day, and the liquid is this bright, electric blue. It stains everything if you spill it. I spilled it once on my favorite white smock, and it looked like a Smurf bled on me. I tried soaking it in bleach, but then the fabric got all weak and tore right at the pocket. Pockets are so important, too, for holding your clips and shears while you work. My shears cost like four hundred dollars. They're Japanese steel, super sharp. You can slice your finger open so easily if you're not paying attention when you're point-cutting. I did that once and had to superglue the cut shut so I could finish my client's blowout. Superglue actually works really well for paper cuts and stuff, too. But um... what was the question? Oh, yeah, feeling bad about myself. Yeah, I just feel like a total failure because I couldn't keep anything together.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

Yeah, I really have. I used to love chatting with my clients, you know? Like, really getting into their lives while I was foiling their hair. And I'd always help out the newer stylists if they were struggling with a formulation. Plus, on my days off, I'd go hiking with my friends all the time. There's this one trail up by the old reservoir that has the most amazing views in the fall. The leaves turn these incredible shades of copper and gold. It's actually a lot like this one custom color I mixed for a client once—half 8G, half 7C, with just a ribbon of red kicker. It was stunning. Color theory is honestly my favorite part of cosmetology. You have to know the color wheel inside and out to neutralize unwanted tones. Like, if someone pulls too warm and their blonde looks brassy, you have to use a violet-based toner to counteract the yellow. Violet cancels yellow, blue cancels orange, green cancels red. It's just basic science, but it feels like magic when you tone a raw, yellow bleach job into this beautiful, icy platinum. We use this one liquid demi-permanent gloss that processes in like, five minutes at the bowl. It's so fast, you literally can't take your eyes off it or it'll grab too dark and look muddy. Muddy blonde is the worst. It just looks dull and lifeless. Which is... I guess kind of how I feel now. Dull. I don't do any of that stuff anymore. I don't hike, I don't help anyone at the salon. I just keep my head down and avoid people. I just don't have that spark in me anymore.
Have you noticed any significant change in your appetite lately?

Um, yeah, I guess so. I've been skipping meals lately without really meaning to, and then I'll realize at night that all I've had the entire day is coffee and maybe a few bites of something. We drink so much coffee at the salon. The owner actually bought this really fancy espresso machine for the break room because we wanted to offer clients like, cappuccinos and lattes while their color processes. It makes such a huge difference in your tips when you hand a client a nice little latte in a real ceramic mug. I tried learning how to do the latte art, you know, like the little leaves and hearts, but it's actually super hard. You have to steam the milk to the exact right microfoam texture, or it just blobs into the cup. And if the milk gets too hot, it scorches and tastes terrible. Burnt milk is the worst smell. It honestly reminds me of when someone's hair gets fried off by a flat iron that's turned up too high. You always have to use a thermal protectant spray before hot tools. Always. Heat damage is completely irreversible, once the protein bonds are shattered, you literally just have to chop it off. It breaks my heart when a girl comes in with her ends just snapping off in the comb like dry spaghetti. But um... yeah, my appetite. I just forget to eat. I've noticed my clothes have gotten a lot looser, too. Like my favorite jeans just sag on me now, and I have to wrap my work apron around my waist twice just to keep it from slipping down.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a symptom-free period of at least two months during the past two years (a criterion for Persistent Depressive Disorder). My symptom profile does not contain a specific item for this, although my depressive episode has only lasted 1 year and 2 months.

Two months is a long time. That's like, almost a whole season. I love when the seasons change, especially fall. Fall is the absolute best time for hair color. Everyone wants to go warmer, you know? Like rich chocolate browns, copper, auburn... it's so gorgeous. The formulas are so fun to mix, it's like painting. We did this one girl last week, she wanted this 'cowboy copper' trend that's all over TikTok right now. Have you seen it? It's like this dusty, muted red-brown. It looked amazing on her, she had these green eyes that just popped. Green eyes are so pretty. My cat has green eyes. His name is Barnaby, and he's a rescue. He's super fluffy, but he sheds everywhere. I have to lint roll my clothes like three times before I leave the house, because you can't show up to the salon covered in cat hair. It just looks unprofessional. Clients notice that stuff. They notice everything, honestly. Like if your nails aren't done, or if your roots are grown out. It's a lot of pressure to always look perfect. But um... yeah, no, I haven't had a good stretch like that in a long time.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been a prior manic or hypomanic episode, which would distinguish major depressive disorder from a bipolar-spectrum depression.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of at least several days when you felt unusually energized or needed much less sleep than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a manic or hypomanic episode (unusual energy, decreased need for sleep), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer: Energized? Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm pretty tired most of the time lately. I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get at least eight hours, I am basically a zombie at the salon. And you cannot be a zombie when you're holding sharp shears right next to someone's ear, you know? It's actually really scary how sharp professional shears are. They're made of this Japanese steel, usually, and they cost like, hundreds of dollars. My first pair was $300, and that was with my student discount. You have to get them sharpened by this special guy who comes to the salon once a month with a little mobile workshop in his van. He's this older guy named Gary, and he always brings donuts. Glazed donuts, which are my favorite, but I try not to eat them because I'm trying to cut back on sugar. Sugar just makes my skin break out so bad, especially around my chin. I read somewhere that chin breakouts are hormonal, but I don't know. Skin care is so confusing. There are a million different serums and acids now. Hyaluronic acid, salicylic acid, glycolic... it's overwhelming. Sometimes I just want to wash my face with regular soap, but my esthetician friend would actually murder me if I did that. She says bar soap destroys your skin barrier. But yeah, no, I've never had a time where I didn't need sleep or felt super energized like that. Just tired.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the depressive episode is attributable to a general medical condition or another medical/neurologic cause rather than primary major depression or persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had any medical illness or injury involving your brain, like a head injury, stroke, seizure disorder, or thyroid problem?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about general medical conditions or neurological/endocrine issues to rule out physiological causes for the symptoms, which is not covered by any specific symptom profile in my list.

patient.answer: Um, no, nothing like that. I've never had a stroke or a seizure or anything wrong with my brain like that. I did hit my head on a cabinet door at the salon once, though. Someone left it open—probably Sarah, she's always leaving the color bar cabinets wide open—and I just stood up right into it. It hurt so bad, I actually saw stars for a second. But I didn't go to the doctor or anything, I just put some ice on it. The ice machine at work is always broken, by the way. It makes this horrible grinding noise, like it's chewing on rocks, and then it just spits out water instead of cubes. We've told the owner, Mr. Davis, like five times, but he's so cheap. He hates spending money on maintenance. He wouldn't even fix the AC last summer until three clients complained that they were sweating through their capes. Those capes get so hot anyway, they don't breathe at all. It's like wearing a trash bag. We try to use the lightweight ones, but they still trap all your body heat. Anyway, no, I haven't had any major head injuries or thyroid things. My thyroid is fine, as far as I know.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has ever been a prior major depressive episode before the current one, to help distinguish recurrent major depressive disorder from persistent depressive disorder and depressive disorder due to another medical condition.
doctor.question: Before this current period of depression, have you ever had another episode of feeling this depressed for at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about previous episodes of depression prior to the current one, which is not specified in the symptom profile.

patient.answer: Um, no, I don't think so. Not before this current time. I mean, I've had bad days here and there, but never two whole weeks in a row of feeling this down. Two weeks is actually exactly how long I tell my clients to wait if they try to cut their own hair at home and mess it up. You know, give it two weeks to grow out just a tiny bit so I have something to work with to fix it. Especially bangs. People get a little sad or bored at 2 AM and suddenly decide they need micro-bangs, and it's always a disaster. Everyone thinks they want bangs right now, like those really cute curtain bangs, but they don't realize how much styling it takes. You have to use a round brush and a blow dryer every single morning, or they just lay flat against your forehead and look super greasy. I always try to warn them, but they never listen. They just bring in a picture from Pinterest and say, 'I want this,' and I have to explain that the girl in the picture has a professional stylist and perfect lighting. Lighting changes everything. We have this huge ring light at the salon for taking Instagram photos of our work, and if you stand in front of it without makeup, you look completely washed out. I actually had to buy this special color-correcting primer just so I wouldn't look dead in the background of my coworkers' photos. It's green, which is so weird to put on your face, but it cancels out the redness. Color theory is actually super interesting, it's basically the whole foundation of doing hair color. But um... what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I haven't had a two-week stretch of feeling like this before.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there is a history of an independent major depressive episode prior to the current one, which would distinguish recurrent major depression from persistent depressive disorder and substance/medication-induced or due-to-medical-condition depression.
doctor.question: Before this current depression, have you ever had another episode like this that lasted at least two weeks?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of previous depressive episodes prior to the current one, which is not covered by the symptom profile that focuses on the current depressive episode and its duration.

patient.answer: Um, I... I think you just asked me that, didn't you? Or wait, did you? My brain is just so foggy right now. But no, I haven't. Not before this time. It's just been this one really long stretch. Kind of like when a client wants to go from box-dye black to platinum blonde in one session. It's just this long, agonizing process, and you're just sitting there waiting for the bleach to lift, hoping their hair doesn't melt off in the foils. Because box dye is the absolute worst. It has all these metallic salts in it that react with professional lightener, and it literally smokes. I saw a girl's hair start smoking once in beauty school. The instructor had to rush over and rinse it out in the bowl, and the smell was horrendous. It smelled like burning tires and sulfur. The bowl area in beauty school was always a mess anyway. The drains were constantly clogged with hair because nobody ever cleaned the traps. It's so gross pulling out those wet clumps of hair. But yeah, no, I haven't had another time like this before. Just this one.

inference.note: Ruled out F06.31 because there is no evidence of a depressive disorder due to another medical condition, and the patient denies relevant neurological/thyroid illness or substance/medication trigger. Symptoms fit a primary depressive disorder; chronicity makes dysthymia/persistent depressive disorder still possible, while the episode duration and lack of prior episodes keep major depressive episode unspecified also possible.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been any period of low mood lasting at least 2 years, which would support dysthymia/persistent depressive disorder over a single major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Have there ever been times during this past year and two months when you felt depressed for at least two months at a stretch?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 2
target_item.manifestation: Looking back, I have spent most of this whole decline feeling depressed and weighed down, with only shorter stretches where the sadness was not as prominent.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the depressive symptoms have been present for the majority of the illness duration (at least two months at a stretch during the past year and two months), which maps to Criterion C of Schizoaffective Disorder.

patient.answer: Um, yeah, I'd say so. Looking back on it, I've spent most of this whole time... like this whole decline over the last year or whatever... feeling really depressed and just weighed down. There were only short stretches where the sadness wasn't as prominent. It's just so heavy, you know? Like when you try to lift a gallon of developer. We buy developer in these massive jugs at the salon to save money, mostly 20 volume because that's what we use the most of for gray coverage. Gray hair is so stubborn. It lacks pigment, obviously, but the cuticle is also super tight, so you really have to pack the color on and sometimes use heat to open it up. A lot of women come in every four weeks on the dot to get their roots touched up. They hate seeing that skunk stripe down their part. I had this one client, Mrs. Higgins, she would come in every three weeks. She was terrified of anyone knowing she wasn't a natural redhead. Red fades the fastest, too. The color molecules are larger than other colors, so they literally slip right out of the hair shaft every time you wash it. That's why I always tell my redheads to wash in cold water. But who wants to take a freezing cold shower? Especially in the winter. Our water heater at my apartment is terrible, so I end up taking cold showers half the time anyway. It takes like twenty minutes for the water to even get lukewarm. But um... yeah, mostly I've just been really depressed this whole time, with only small breaks.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has chronic low self-esteem, which would support dysthymia (persistent depressive disorder) over a single major depressive episode.
doctor.question: Do you often feel like a failure or feel bad about yourself?

target_item.name: Worthlessness_Guilt
target_item.manifestation: I keep thinking I’m a burden on everyone and that I deserve what’s happening because I couldn’t keep my money, my job, or even basic salon responsibilities together.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel like a failure or feel bad about myself, which directly maps to feelings of worthlessness or guilt.

patient.answer: Yeah, all the time. I just... I keep thinking I'm a burden on everyone. Like I completely deserve all of this happening to me because I couldn't even keep my money straight or hold onto my job. I couldn't even manage basic salon responsibilities, you know? Like sweeping up hair or keeping my station sanitized. State board is so strict about sanitation. If an inspector walks in and sees a single hair on your clippers or a comb sitting on the counter instead of in the Barbicide, they can fine you on the spot. The Barbicide jar has to be changed every single day, and the liquid is this bright, electric blue. It stains everything if you spill it. I spilled it once on my favorite white smock, and it looked like a Smurf bled on me. I tried soaking it in bleach, but then the fabric got all weak and tore right at the pocket. Pockets are so important, too, for holding your clips and shears while you work. My shears cost like four hundred dollars. They're Japanese steel, super sharp. You can slice your finger open so easily if you're not paying attention when you're point-cutting. I did that once and had to superglue the cut shut so I could finish my client's blowout. Superglue actually works really well for paper cuts and stuff, too. But um... what was the question? Oh, yeah, feeling bad about myself. Yeah, I just feel like a total failure because I couldn't keep anything together.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the patient has persistent loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), which would support major depressive disorder over persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Negative_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I used to chat with clients, help the newer stylists, and go hiking with friends, but now I mostly keep my head down and avoid people because I just don’t have that spark in me.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about losing interest or pleasure in previously enjoyed activities corresponds to negative symptoms, specifically avolition/anhedonia, which involves a loss of motivation or social interest.

patient.answer: Yeah, I really have. I used to love chatting with my clients, you know? Like, really getting into their lives while I was foiling their hair. And I'd always help out the newer stylists if they were struggling with a formulation. Plus, on my days off, I'd go hiking with my friends all the time. There's this one trail up by the old reservoir that has the most amazing views in the fall. The leaves turn these incredible shades of copper and gold. It's actually a lot like this one custom color I mixed for a client once—half 8G, half 7C, with just a ribbon of red kicker. It was stunning. Color theory is honestly my favorite part of cosmetology. You have to know the color wheel inside and out to neutralize unwanted tones. Like, if someone pulls too warm and their blonde looks brassy, you have to use a violet-based toner to counteract the yellow. Violet cancels yellow, blue cancels orange, green cancels red. It's just basic science, but it feels like magic when you tone a raw, yellow bleach job into this beautiful, icy platinum. We use this one liquid demi-permanent gloss that processes in like, five minutes at the bowl. It's so fast, you literally can't take your eyes off it or it'll grab too dark and look muddy. Muddy blonde is the worst. It just looks dull and lifeless. Which is... I guess kind of how I feel now. Dull. I don't do any of that stuff anymore. I don't hike, I don't help anyone at the salon. I just keep my head down and avoid people. I just don't have that spark in me anymore.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the depressive syndrome includes neurovegetative/appetite change, which helps distinguish major depressive disorder from persistent depressive disorder and further characterize episode severity.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant change in your appetite lately?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been skipping meals without really meaning to, then realizing at night I only had coffee and a few bites of something, and my clothes have gotten looser.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite, which maps directly to the Weight_Appetite_Change symptom.

patient.answer: Um, yeah, I guess so. I've been skipping meals lately without really meaning to, and then I'll realize at night that all I've had the entire day is coffee and maybe a few bites of something. We drink so much coffee at the salon. The owner actually bought this really fancy espresso machine for the break room because we wanted to offer clients like, cappuccinos and lattes while their color processes. It makes such a huge difference in your tips when you hand a client a nice little latte in a real ceramic mug. I tried learning how to do the latte art, you know, like the little leaves and hearts, but it's actually super hard. You have to steam the milk to the exact right microfoam texture, or it just blobs into the cup. And if the milk gets too hot, it scorches and tastes terrible. Burnt milk is the worst smell. It honestly reminds me of when someone's hair gets fried off by a flat iron that's turned up too high. You always have to use a thermal protectant spray before hot tools. Always. Heat damage is completely irreversible, once the protein bonds are shattered, you literally just have to chop it off. It breaks my heart when a girl comes in with her ends just snapping off in the comb like dry spaghetti. But um... yeah, my appetite. I just forget to eat. I've noticed my clothes have gotten a lot looser, too. Like my favorite jeans just sag on me now, and I have to wrap my work apron around my waist twice just to keep it from slipping down.
